why_use_this:
This is the broadest statistics toolbox in the vani-* ecosystem -- reach for it for descriptive statistics, probability distributions (PMF/PDF/CDF), correlation and regression, information theory, hypothesis testing (test statistics AND p-values), Bayesian inference, Markov chains, time series analysis, and a few stochastic-process/dimensionality-reduction tools that lean on [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix) (multiple regression, PCA, Kalman filtering). If you need a specific distribution's PDF/PMF and its CDF, they're paired by name (`gamma_pdf`/`gamma_cdf`, `chi_squared_pdf`/`chi_squared_cdf`, ...) -- and where a test statistic exists, its matching p-value function is also paired by name (`t_stat_one_sample` feeds `t_pvalue_two_tailed`, `chi_squared_stat` feeds `chi_squared_pvalue`, ...), so you're rarely more than one function call away from turning a raw statistic into an actual decision. For anything already covered by a compiler builtin (`f64_normal_pdf`/`_cdf`, `rand_normal`, `f64_erf`, `i64_factorial`/`_binomial`, ...) this package deliberately does NOT duplicate it -- call the builtin directly.

A few small running datasets thread through the notes below: \(D_1=(2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9)\) (a classic textbook example with mean exactly 5) for descriptive statistics; \(x=(1,2,3,4,5)\), \(y=(2,4,5,4,5)\) for correlation/regression; and a classic medical-test scenario (a rare disease, a 99%-accurate test) for Bayesian inference.

mean.intuition: Add everything up, divide by how many there are -- the single most familiar "average".
mean.why: This exact dataset and mean (\(5\)) is a well-known textbook example specifically because the numbers work out clean -- every other descriptive-statistic note below reuses it.

variance.intuition: How spread out are the values around the mean, on average? Squaring each deviation before averaging makes sure positive and negative deviations don't cancel out, and penalizes big deviations more than small ones.
variance.example: \(D_1\), mean \(5\): squared deviations are \(9,1,1,1,0,0,4,16\) (summing to \(32\)). Sample variance \(=32/(8-1)=32/7\approx4.571\).
variance.why: Dividing by \(n-1\) (not \(n\)) is the Bessel correction -- using the SAMPLE mean (rather than the unknown true population mean) to compute deviations slightly underestimates the true spread, and dividing by \(n-1\) instead of \(n\) corrects for that bias.

std_dev.intuition: Variance is in SQUARED units (e.g. "dollars squared"), which is awkward to interpret -- taking the square root brings it back to the original units.
std_dev.why: This is the number that shows up directly in `z_stat`/`t_stat_one_sample`'s denominators -- "how many standard deviations away from the mean" is a far more interpretable quantity than raw squared-units variance.

median.intuition: The middle value when everything is sorted -- unlike the mean, a few extreme outliers can't drag the median far from where "most" of the data actually sits.
median.formula: The middle value (or average of the two middle values, for an even count) of the sorted sample.
median.example: \(D_1\) sorted is already \((2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9)\), \(n=8\) (even): average the 4th and 5th values, \(4\) and \(5\): median \(=(4+5)/2=4.5\) -- notice this is slightly LESS than the mean (\(5\)), because the single large value \(9\) pulls the mean up more than it affects the median.
median.why: This \(4.5\) vs. the mean's \(5\) is a concrete, small-scale illustration of why median is preferred over mean for skewed data (like income or house prices) where a few extreme values would otherwise dominate the average.

skewness.intuition: Is the data's tail longer on the right or the left? Cubing (rather than squaring) the deviations preserves their SIGN, so a few large positive deviations (a long right tail) push this measure positive, and vice versa.
skewness.example: \(D_1\), using population moments (\(\sigma=2\) for this exact dataset): cubed deviations are \(-27,-3,-3,-3,0,0,8,64\) (summing to \(36\)). Skewness \(\approx(36/8)/2^3=4.5/8=0.5625\) -- positive, correctly reflecting that \(D_1\) has a longer tail toward the high end (the \(7\) and especially the \(9\)) than toward the low end.
skewness.why: A skewness near \(0\) suggests roughly symmetric data (like a normal distribution); this dataset's clearly positive value quantifies the visible asymmetry -- three values tied at \(4\) near the low-middle, but only one high outlier at \(9\) rather than a matching low outlier.

kurtosis.intuition: How heavy are the tails, and how sharp is the peak, compared to a normal distribution? Raising deviations to the 4th power weights extreme values even more heavily than skewness's cubing does.
kurtosis.example: \(D_1\), population moments: 4th-power deviations are \(81,1,1,1,0,0,16,256\) (summing to \(356\)). Kurtosis \(\approx(356/8)/2^4=44.5/16\approx2.78\) -- close to (though slightly under) the normal distribution's reference value of \(3\), suggesting tails not too different from normal despite the visible skew.
kurtosis.why: This is RAW kurtosis (not "excess kurtosis", which would subtract 3) -- a value of exactly 3 would indicate normal-like tail weight; noticeably above 3 means heavier tails (more extreme outliers than normal); below 3 means lighter tails.

weighted_mean.intuition: An ordinary mean treats every value equally; a weighted mean lets some values count more than others -- like a grade average where a final exam counts more than a homework assignment.
weighted_mean.example: Values \((2,4)\) with weights \((1,3)\) (the second value counts 3 times as much): \(\dfrac{1\times2+3\times4}{1+3}=\dfrac{2+12}4=\dfrac{14}4=3.5\) -- pulled much closer to \(4\) than a plain unweighted mean (\(3\)) would be, exactly because \(4\) carries more weight.
weighted_mean.why: Setting every weight to \(1\) reduces this formula exactly to the plain `mean` -- weighted mean is a strict generalization, not a different computation.

weighted_variance.intuition: The weighted analog of `variance` -- spread around the WEIGHTED mean, with each squared deviation itself weighted too.
weighted_variance.example: Same values/weights as `weighted_mean`'s example, \(\bar x_w=3.5\): weighted squared deviations are \(1\times(2-3.5)^2=2.25\) and \(3\times(4-3.5)^2=0.75\), summing to \(3\). \(W=4\), \(W_2=1^2+3^2=10\). Denominator \(=4-10/4=1.5\). Weighted variance \(=3/1.5=2\).
weighted_variance.why: This denominator is a generalized Bessel correction -- when every weight equals \(1\) (so \(W=n\), \(W_2=n\)), the denominator reduces exactly to \(n-1\), recovering ordinary sample variance as a special case.

quantile.intuition: Generalizes the median to any percentage cutoff -- the median is just the special case of asking for the 50th percentile.
quantile.formula: The value below which a fraction \(q\) of the (sorted) sample falls.
quantile.example: For \(D_1\), `quantile` at \(q=0.5\) should agree with `median`'s own answer, \(4.5\) -- a direct built-in consistency check between the two functions.
quantile.why: Reach for arbitrary quantiles (not just the median) when you want to describe more of a distribution's shape -- e.g. the 10th and 90th percentiles together describe where the middle 80% of the data sits, useful for spotting outliers or characterizing spread beyond what a single median captures.

iqr.intuition: The range covering the middle 50% of the data -- the gap between the 25th and 75th percentiles -- a robust measure of spread that isn't dragged around by a few extreme outliers the way the full range (max minus min) would be.
iqr.example: For \(D_1=(2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9)\): the middle half of the data (excluding the lowest and highest quarters) sits roughly between the low \(4\)s and the \(5\)s/\(7\), giving a modest IQR -- notably smaller than the full range (\(9-2=7\)), since the IQR deliberately ignores the extremes.
iqr.why: This is the same robust-to-outliers idea `median` has over `mean` -- a single very large or very small value can drastically change the full range, but barely budges the IQR at all, since it only ever touches the middle half of the data.

mode.intuition: The single most commonly occurring value -- useful for categorical-feeling data, or for spotting a genuinely repeated "typical" value that mean/median wouldn't highlight.
mode.formula: The most frequently occurring value in the sample.
mode.example: \(D_1=(2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9)\): \(4\) appears three times (more than any other value, which appear at most twice), so the mode is \(4\).
mode.why: Notice mode (\(4\)), median (\(4.5\)), and mean (\(5\)) are all DIFFERENT numbers for this same dataset -- a concrete reminder that "average" isn't one single well-defined concept; which of the three you want depends on what question you're actually asking.

binomial_pmf.intuition: How likely is it to get EXACTLY \(k\) successes out of \(n\) independent yes/no trials, each with success probability \(p\)? Count how many different ORDERS could produce \(k\) successes (the binomial coefficient), then multiply by the probability of any one specific order.
binomial_pmf.example: \(n=10\) coin-flip-like trials, \(p=0.3\), exactly \(k=3\) successes: \(\binom{10}3=120\), \(0.3^3=0.027\), \(0.7^7\approx0.08235\). \(P(X=3)=120\times0.027\times0.08235\approx0.2668\) -- about a 26.7% chance of exactly 3 successes.
binomial_pmf.why: This exact scenario (\(n=10,p=0.3\)) reappears in `binomial_cdf`'s example, which sums this and the surrounding probabilities together to answer a related "at most" question instead of "exactly".

binomial_cdf.intuition: Instead of "exactly \(k\) successes", answer "AT MOST \(k\) successes" -- add up the individual probabilities for every count from \(0\) up to \(k\).
binomial_cdf.example: Same \(n=10,p=0.3\), \(k=3\): \(P(X{=}0)\approx0.0282\), \(P(X{=}1)\approx0.1211\), \(P(X{=}2)\approx0.2335\), \(P(X{=}3)\approx0.2668\) (from `binomial_pmf`'s example). Sum: \(P(X\le3)\approx0.0282+0.1211+0.2335+0.2668\approx0.6496\) -- about a 65% chance of 3 or fewer successes.
binomial_cdf.why: Notice \(P(X\le3)\approx0.65\) is far bigger than \(P(X{=}3)\approx0.27\) alone -- a common mistake is to confuse a PMF (one specific outcome's probability) with a CDF (the cumulative probability up to and including that outcome); they answer genuinely different questions.

poisson_pmf.intuition: Models the count of independent, randomly-timed events (customer arrivals, radioactive decays, typos per page) given only their AVERAGE rate -- unlike the binomial, there's no fixed number of "trials", just a rate.
poisson_pmf.example: Average rate \(\lambda=2\) events per interval, probability of exactly \(k=3\): \(\dfrac{2^3e^{-2}}{3!}=\dfrac{8\times0.1353}{6}\approx\dfrac{1.0827}{6}\approx0.1804\) -- about 18%.
poisson_pmf.why: The Poisson distribution is actually the LIMIT of the binomial as \(n\to\infty\) and \(p\to0\) while \(np=\lambda\) stays fixed -- it's what you get when there are effectively unlimited "trials" (any instant could have an event) but each individual instant's probability is vanishingly small.

poisson_cdf.intuition: Same "sum up to and including \(k\)" idea as `binomial_cdf`, for the Poisson distribution.
poisson_cdf.example: Same \(\lambda=2\), \(k=3\): \(P(X{=}0)\approx0.1353\), \(P(X{=}1)\approx0.2707\), \(P(X{=}2)\approx0.2707\), \(P(X{=}3)\approx0.1804\) (from `poisson_pmf`'s example). Sum: \(P(X\le3)\approx0.8571\) -- about 86% chance of 3 or fewer events.
poisson_cdf.why: Notice \(P(X{=}1)\) and \(P(X{=}2)\) come out EQUAL (\(\approx0.2707\) each) for \(\lambda=2\) -- a specific property of the Poisson distribution's shape (its mode straddles \(\lambda\) when \(\lambda\) is a whole number, here tied between \(k=1\) and \(k=2\)).

geometric_pmf.intuition: How many independent yes/no trials until the FIRST success? This asks for the probability that the first success happens on EXACTLY trial \(k\) -- meaning trials \(1\) through \(k-1\) all failed, and then trial \(k\) succeeded.
geometric_pmf.example: Success probability \(p=0.25\), probability the first success is exactly on trial \(k=3\): \((1-0.25)^{2}\times0.25 = 0.75^2\times0.25=0.5625\times0.25=0.140625\) -- about 14%.
geometric_pmf.why: This is the DISCRETE analog of `exponential_pdf` -- both describe "waiting time until the next event", just in discrete trial-counted steps versus continuous time.

geometric_cdf.intuition: Rather than summing individual pmf terms, the geometric distribution has a direct closed-form shortcut: the probability the first success happens by trial \(k\) is just \(1\) minus the probability of \(k\) STRAIGHT failures.
geometric_cdf.example: Same \(p=0.25\), \(k=3\): \(1-0.75^3=1-0.421875=0.578125\) -- about 58% chance the first success happens within the first 3 trials.
geometric_cdf.why: Unlike `binomial_cdf`/`poisson_cdf` (which genuinely need to sum several terms), the geometric distribution's CDF has this clean closed form -- no summation loop needed at all, computed directly.

negative_binomial_pmf.intuition: Generalizes `geometric_pmf` from waiting for the FIRST success to waiting for the \(r\)-th success -- how likely is it that the \(r\)-th success happens on exactly trial \(k\)?
negative_binomial_pmf.example: Waiting for the 2nd success (\(r=2\)) with \(p=0.3\), probability it happens on exactly trial \(k=5\): \(\binom41\times0.3^2\times0.7^3 = 4\times0.09\times0.343=4\times0.03087=0.12348\) -- about 12%.
negative_binomial_pmf.why: Setting \(r=1\) reduces this exactly to `geometric_pmf`'s formula -- negative binomial is the strict generalization, waiting for the FIRST success being just a special case of waiting for the \(r\)-th.

hypergeometric_pmf.intuition: Like the binomial distribution, but for drawing WITHOUT replacement from a finite population -- once you've drawn a "success" item, it's gone, so the probability of drawing another success shifts as you go, unlike independent binomial trials.
hypergeometric_pmf.example: A population of \(N=10\) items, \(K=4\) of them "successes"; draw \(n=3\) without replacement, probability of exactly \(k=2\) successes: \(\dfrac{\binom42\binom61}{\binom{10}3} = \dfrac{6\times6}{120}=\dfrac{36}{120}=0.3\) -- 30%.
hypergeometric_pmf.why: The classic real-world example: drawing cards from a deck, balls from an urn, or a quality-control sample from a finite batch -- anywhere "drawing without putting back" applies, `binomial_pmf` would be the WRONG tool (it assumes independence, which sampling without replacement violates).

exponential_pdf.intuition: Models the waiting time until the next event in a Poisson process (the continuous-time cousin of `geometric_pmf`) -- higher rate \(\lambda\) means events happen sooner on average, so the density is highest at \(t=0\) and decays smoothly.
exponential_pdf.why: This exact value, \(\approx0.1839\), reappears in `chi_squared_pdf`'s, `gamma_pdf`'s, and `laplace_pdf`'s examples too -- all four distributions were deliberately given parameters that make them evaluate to the SAME number at their respective example points, a concrete illustration of how these distributions relate to (or specialize into) each other.

exponential_cdf.intuition: The probability the wait is AT MOST \(x\) -- has a clean closed form, unlike `poisson_cdf`'s summation.
exponential_cdf.why: This exact value, \(0.6321\), reappears in `chi_squared_cdf`'s and `gamma_cdf`'s examples -- all evaluating the SAME underlying exponential-shaped tail probability via three different (but for these specific parameter choices, mathematically equivalent) distribution families.

uniform_pdf.intuition: Every value in the interval \([a,b]\) is equally likely -- flat density, zero everywhere else.
uniform_pdf.example: \(a=0,b=4\), density at any point in range (e.g. \(x=1\)): \(\dfrac1{4-0}=0.25\) -- the SAME value regardless of exactly where \(x\) falls within \([0,4]\).
uniform_pdf.why: This constant-density property is what makes `uniform_cdf` below come out as a simple straight LINE rather than any curve -- equal density everywhere means probability accumulates at a constant rate as \(x\) increases.

uniform_cdf.intuition: Since the density is flat, the cumulative probability grows in a straight line -- twice as far into the interval means twice the accumulated probability.
uniform_cdf.example: Same \(a=0,b=4\), at \(x=1\): \(\dfrac{1-0}{4-0}=0.25\) -- exactly 25% of the way through the interval, exactly 25% of the accumulated probability, the hallmark of a uniform distribution's linear CDF.
uniform_cdf.why: Compare this straight-line CDF against `exponential_cdf`'s curved one -- the uniform distribution is the one continuous distribution whose CDF is a simple line, a direct visual signature of "every value equally likely".

t_pdf.intuition: Looks like the familiar bell-shaped normal distribution, but with heavier tails -- reflecting the extra uncertainty that comes from estimating a population's standard deviation from a SAMPLE (rather than knowing it exactly), which is more consequential when the sample is small (few degrees of freedom).
t_pdf.formula: The Student's t-distribution density with `df` degrees of freedom.
t_pdf.example: With very few degrees of freedom (e.g. `df=2`), the peak at \(x=0\) is noticeably LOWER and the tails noticeably FATTER than a standard normal's peak (\(\approx0.399\)) -- as `df` grows large, the t-distribution's shape converges toward the standard normal's.
t_pdf.why: This is exactly why `t_stat_one_sample`/`t_stat_two_sample`'s test statistics get compared against the t-distribution (via `t_cdf`) rather than the normal distribution -- the extra tail weight correctly accounts for the added uncertainty of an ESTIMATED standard deviation, especially significant for small samples.

beta_pdf.intuition: Models a probability or proportion itself as an uncertain quantity, constrained to live in \([0,1]\) -- shape parameters \(\alpha,\beta\) control where the density concentrates: equal \(\alpha=\beta\) centers it symmetrically at \(0.5\).
beta_pdf.example: \(\alpha=\beta=2\) (symmetric), density at \(x=0.5\): \(\dfrac{\Gamma(4)}{\Gamma(2)\Gamma(2)}\times0.5^1\times0.5^1 = 6\times0.25=1.5\) -- notice this is ABOVE 1, which is fine (unlike a probability, a density value itself isn't bounded by 1).
beta_pdf.why: The Beta distribution is the natural conjugate prior for a binomial's success probability in Bayesian inference -- start with a Beta prior belief about an unknown probability, observe binomial data, and the updated (posterior) belief is again exactly a Beta distribution, with parameters shifted by the observed successes/failures.

chi_squared_pdf.intuition: The distribution of a sum of \(k\) squared independent standard-normal values -- shows up constantly in hypothesis testing (`chi_squared_stat`'s test statistic is compared against this distribution) because sums of squared deviations naturally follow this shape.
chi_squared_pdf.formula: The chi-squared density with \(k\) degrees of freedom.
chi_squared_pdf.example: With \(k=2\) specifically, chi-squared has a special closed form -- it's IDENTICAL to `exponential_pdf` with \(\lambda=0.5\): at \(x=2\), \(\tfrac12e^{-1}\approx0.1839\) -- exactly matching `exponential_pdf`'s example value.
chi_squared_pdf.why: This \(k=2\) case being exactly exponential isn't a coincidence -- the chi-squared distribution with 2 degrees of freedom IS mathematically the exponential distribution with rate \(1/2\), a genuine special-case identity between the two distribution families, not just numerically similar parameters.

gamma_pdf.intuition: Generalizes the exponential distribution to model the waiting time for MULTIPLE events, not just one -- `shape` controls how many events you're waiting for, `rate` controls how frequently they happen.
gamma_pdf.example: With `shape=1` specifically, the Gamma distribution reduces exactly to the exponential: at `rate=0.5`, \(x=2\): \(\dfrac{0.5^1}{\Gamma(1)}\times x^0\times e^{-0.5\times2} = 0.5\times1\times e^{-1}\approx0.1839\) -- exactly matching `exponential_pdf`'s and `chi_squared_pdf`'s example values.
gamma_pdf.why: This three-way match (`exponential_pdf`, `chi_squared_pdf` at \(k=2\), and `gamma_pdf` at `shape=1`) is a genuine chain of special-case identities: Gamma(shape=1) IS Exponential, and Exponential(rate=0.5) IS Chi-squared(k=2) -- three names for closely related (here, identical) distributions, each emphasizing a different interpretation.

laplace_pdf.intuition: Two exponential decays glued back-to-back at the center \(\mu\) -- sometimes called the "double exponential" for exactly this reason, giving a sharp peak (unlike the normal distribution's smooth rounded top) with heavier tails than a normal of the same spread.
laplace_pdf.example: \(\mu=0,b=1\), density at \(x=1\): \(\dfrac1{2}e^{-|1-0|/1}=0.5\times e^{-1}\approx0.1839\) -- yet again matching `exponential_pdf`'s example value, since at this specific point the Laplace density's formula reduces to the same \(0.5e^{-1}\) computation.
laplace_pdf.why: The sharp peak at \(\mu\) (a discontinuous change in slope, unlike the normal distribution's smooth peak) makes the Laplace distribution useful for modeling data with a strong central tendency but occasional larger deviations -- and it's the maximum-likelihood-motivated distribution behind L1 (absolute-value) regression loss, the way the normal distribution underlies ordinary least-squares (L2) regression.

log_normal_pdf.intuition: Models a quantity whose LOGARITHM is normally distributed -- common for anything that's the PRODUCT of many independent positive factors (stock prices, biological measurements), the multiplicative analog of how a normal distribution arises from many independent ADDITIVE factors.
log_normal_pdf.example: \(\mu=0,\sigma=1\), density at \(x=1\): since \(\ln(1)=0=\mu\) exactly, this point sits right at the underlying normal distribution's own peak: \(\dfrac1{1\times1\times\sqrt{2\pi}}\times e^0 = \dfrac1{2.5066}\approx0.3989\) -- exactly the standard normal distribution's peak density.
log_normal_pdf.why: Unlike the normal distribution, log-normal is only defined for POSITIVE \(x\) (since you can't take the logarithm of a non-positive number) -- a natural fit for quantities that are physically constrained to be positive (prices, concentrations, sizes) where a plain normal distribution could nonsensically predict negative values.

covariance.intuition: Do two variables tend to move together (both above average at the same time) or oppositely? Multiply each pair's deviations from their own means -- both-positive or both-negative pairs contribute positively, opposite-sign pairs contribute negatively.
covariance.example: \(x=(1,2,3,4,5)\), \(y=(2,4,5,4,5)\) (means \(\bar x=3,\bar y=4\)): paired deviation products are \((-2)(-2)=4\), \((-1)(0)=0\), \((0)(1)=0\), \((1)(0)=0\), \((2)(1)=2\), summing to \(6\). Covariance \(=6/4=1.5\) -- positive, confirming \(x\) and \(y\) tend to move together.
covariance.why: This exact \((x,y)\) pair and its covariance (\(1.5\)) reappear throughout `pearson_r`, `ols_slope`, and `ols_r_squared`'s examples below -- all downstream of this one covariance computation.

pearson_r.intuition: Covariance alone doesn't say whether an association is STRONG or weak, since it depends on the variables' own scales -- dividing by both standard deviations normalizes it into a scale-free number always between \(-1\) and \(1\).
pearson_r.example: Same \(x,y\): covariance \(1.5\) (from `covariance`'s example). \(s_x=\sqrt{2.5}\approx1.581\), \(s_y=\sqrt{1.5}\approx1.225\). \(r=1.5/(1.581\times1.225)\approx1.5/1.936\approx0.775\) -- a fairly strong positive linear association.
pearson_r.why: This same \(r\approx0.775\), squared, gives \(\approx0.6\) -- exactly `ols_r_squared`'s answer for the identical data, confirming the shortcut \(R^2=r^2\) that only holds for SIMPLE (one-predictor) linear regression.

ols_slope.intuition: The best-fit line's steepness -- how much does \(y\) tend to change for each unit increase in \(x\)?
ols_slope.why: This \(0.6\) feeds directly into `ols_intercept`'s example -- slope first, then intercept is chosen so the fitted line passes through the point of means.

ols_intercept.intuition: Once the slope is fixed, the intercept is whatever value makes the line pass exactly through the point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) -- the "center of mass" of the data.
ols_intercept.example: \(\bar y=4\), \(\hat\beta_1=0.6\) (from `ols_slope`), \(\bar x=3\): intercept \(=4-0.6\times3=4-1.8=2.2\). So the fitted line is \(\hat y=2.2+0.6x\) -- check it passes through \((3,4)\): \(2.2+0.6\times3=2.2+1.8=4.0\), confirmed.
ols_intercept.why: This guarantee (the fitted line ALWAYS passes through the point of means) is a direct mathematical consequence of how ordinary least squares is derived -- not a coincidence, but baked into the method.

ols_r_squared.intuition: For SIMPLE (one-predictor) regression specifically, there's a shortcut: the coefficient of determination is just Pearson's correlation coefficient, squared.
ols_r_squared.example: \(r\approx0.775\) (from `pearson_r`'s example): \(R^2\approx0.775^2\approx0.6\) -- the model explains about 60% of \(y\)'s variance.
ols_r_squared.why: This shortcut ONLY works for simple regression with exactly one predictor -- [vani-ml](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-ml)'s `mlr_r_squared` (for MULTIPLE predictors) has to compute \(R^2\) the general way, from actual residuals, since there's no single correlation coefficient to square once more than one predictor is involved.

shannon_entropy.intuition: How unpredictable is an outcome drawn from this distribution, on average? A distribution concentrated on one outcome has zero entropy (no surprise, you already know the answer); a spread-out (uniform) distribution has maximum entropy (every outcome is a genuine surprise).
shannon_entropy.example: A fair coin, \(p=(0.5,0.5)\): \(H=-(0.5\ln0.5+0.5\ln0.5)=-\ln0.5\approx0.693\) nats (or, in base-2, exactly 1 bit -- the maximum possible entropy for a 2-outcome distribution).
shannon_entropy.why: A fair coin has the MAXIMUM possible entropy among all 2-outcome distributions -- any bias (e.g. \(p=(0.9,0.1)\)) makes the outcome more predictable and entropy correspondingly lower, down to \(0\) for a completely certain (100%/0%) outcome.

kl_divergence.intuition: How much "extra surprise" do you incur by believing distribution \(Q\) when the true distribution is actually \(P\)? Zero when \(P\) and \(Q\) are identical, growing as they diverge -- but NOT symmetric: the cost of mistaking \(P\) for \(Q\) isn't generally the same as mistaking \(Q\) for \(P\).
kl_divergence.why: This \(0.511\) reappears directly in `cross_entropy`'s example -- cross-entropy is defined as exactly `shannon_entropy`'s value PLUS this KL divergence, a relationship confirmed numerically there.

cross_entropy.intuition: The total "surprise" of using distribution \(Q\)'s predictions to describe outcomes actually drawn from \(P\) -- decomposes cleanly into \(P\)'s own inherent unpredictability (`shannon_entropy`) plus the EXTRA cost specifically from \(Q\) being wrong (`kl_divergence`).
cross_entropy.example: Same \(P=(0.5,0.5)\), \(Q=(0.9,0.1)\): direct computation, \(-[0.5\ln0.9+0.5\ln0.1] = -[0.5\times(-0.105)+0.5\times(-2.303)]=-[-0.053-1.151]=1.204\). Cross-check via the decomposition: \(H(P)+D_{KL}(P\Vert Q)\approx0.693+0.511=1.204\) -- matches exactly.
cross_entropy.why: This is exactly the loss function [vani-ml](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-ml)'s `graph_binary_cross_entropy_loss` implements as a differentiable graph node -- training a classifier to minimize cross-entropy is training it to make \(Q\) (the model's predicted distribution) match \(P\) (the true label distribution) as closely as possible.

renyi_entropy.intuition: A dial that generalizes Shannon entropy: different values of \(\alpha\) weight rare vs. common outcomes differently -- Shannon entropy is the special limiting case as \(\alpha\to1\).
renyi_entropy.example: Fair coin \(P=(0.5,0.5)\), \(\alpha=2\): \(\sum p_i^2=0.25+0.25=0.5\). \(H_2=\dfrac1{1-2}\ln(0.5) = -1\times(-0.693)=0.693\) -- EXACTLY matching `shannon_entropy`'s answer for this same distribution.
renyi_entropy.why: This exact match isn't a coincidence specific to \(\alpha=2\) -- for a UNIFORM distribution specifically (every outcome equally likely, as the fair coin is), Renyi entropy gives the same answer regardless of \(\alpha\); the different weightings only produce different answers when the distribution is non-uniform.

t_stat_one_sample.intuition: Is this sample's mean surprisingly far from a hypothesized value, given how much natural spread the sample already shows? Measured in units of "estimated standard errors", so it's comparable across problems with different scales.
t_stat_one_sample.why: This \(t\approx1.32\) would get compared against the t-distribution (via `t_cdf`, then `t_pvalue_two_tailed`) with \(n-1=7\) degrees of freedom to decide whether this difference from \(\mu_0=4\) is large enough to call statistically significant, or plausibly just sampling noise.

t_stat_two_sample.intuition: The same idea as `t_stat_one_sample`, comparing TWO independent samples' means to each other instead of one sample's mean to a fixed hypothesized value.
t_stat_two_sample.formula: Compares two independent samples' means, using pooled (or Welch-adjusted) variance in the standard-error denominator.
t_stat_two_sample.example: Two small samples, \(x=(1,2,3)\) (mean \(2\), variance \(1\)) and \(y=(4,5,6)\) (mean \(5\), variance \(1\)): using `pooled_variance`'s matching example (pooled variance \(=1\)), \(t=\dfrac{2-5}{\sqrt{1\times(1/3+1/3)}}=\dfrac{-3}{\sqrt{0.667}}\approx\dfrac{-3}{0.816}\approx-3.67\) -- a large-magnitude \(t\), correctly reflecting that these two samples' means are quite far apart relative to their spread.
t_stat_two_sample.why: The SIGN of \(t\) (negative here) just reflects which sample's mean is larger -- what matters for significance testing is the MAGNITUDE, |t|, which `t_pvalue_two_tailed` uses directly.

chi_squared_stat.intuition: How far off are your OBSERVED category counts from what you EXPECTED, relative to how much variation you'd expect just from chance? Squaring each gap (and dividing by the expected count) keeps every category's contribution positive and appropriately scaled.
chi_squared_stat.why: The third category contributed exactly \(0\) (observed exactly matched expected there) -- only categories with a genuine observed-vs-expected gap add to the statistic, and bigger gaps in categories with SMALLER expected counts count disproportionately more (dividing by a smaller \(E_i\)).

z_stat.intuition: Like `t_stat_one_sample`, but for the (less realistic, but simpler) case where the population's TRUE standard deviation is already known exactly, not estimated from the sample.
z_stat.example: \(D_1\), mean \(5\), \(n=8\), testing against \(\mu_0=4\), with a KNOWN population \(\sigma=2\) (rather than the sample's own estimated \(s\approx2.138\)): \(z=\dfrac{5-4}{2/\sqrt8}=\dfrac1{0.7071}\approx1.414\).
z_stat.why: Compare this \(z\approx1.414\) against `t_stat_one_sample`'s \(t\approx1.323\) on the same data -- they're close but not identical, because \(z\) uses the assumed-known \(\sigma=2\) while \(t\) uses the sample's own estimated \(s\approx2.138\); as sample size grows, this gap between \(z\) and \(t\) statistics shrinks.

conditional_prob.intuition: Given that you already know event \(B\) happened, how likely is event \(A\)? Restrict attention to only the cases where \(B\) occurred, and ask what fraction of THOSE also have \(A\).
conditional_prob.why: This is the basic building block `bayes_posterior`/`law_of_total_prob` below both build on -- Bayesian inference is fundamentally about computing conditional probabilities in the "backwards" direction (effect back to cause) from ones you can more easily state directly (cause to effect).

law_of_total_prob.intuition: If you don't know which of several mutually-exclusive scenarios is true, an event's OVERALL probability is the weighted average of its probability under each scenario, weighted by how likely each scenario is.
law_of_total_prob.example: A rare disease affects 1% of a population (prior \(=0.01\) disease, \(0.99\) no disease). A test is 99% sensitive (\(P(\text{positive}\mid\text{disease})=0.99\)) and has a 5% false-positive rate (\(P(\text{positive}\mid\text{no disease})=0.05\)). Overall probability of testing positive: \(P(\text{positive}) = 0.01\times0.99+0.99\times0.05 = 0.0099+0.0495=0.0594\) -- about 5.94% of the ENTIRE population (disease or not) would test positive.
law_of_total_prob.why: This \(0.0594\) is exactly the normalizing denominator `bayes_posterior`/`normalize_probs`'s example uses next, to answer the much more interesting REVERSE question: given a positive test, how likely is the disease actually present?

bayes_posterior.intuition: Combine what you believed BEFORE seeing evidence (the prior) with how well each hypothesis explains the evidence you actually saw (the likelihood) -- multiply them together, hypothesis by hypothesis.
bayes_posterior.example: Same medical-test scenario: priors \((0.01,\,0.99)\) for (disease, no disease); likelihoods of testing positive, \((0.99,\,0.05)\). Unnormalized posterior: \((0.01\times0.99,\ 0.99\times0.05) = (0.0099,\ 0.0495)\).
bayes_posterior.why: These two numbers, \(0.0099\) and \(0.0495\), don't sum to \(1\) -- they're not yet a valid probability distribution, just relative weights. `normalize_probs`'s example below rescales them into the ACTUAL posterior probabilities.

normalize_probs.intuition: Rescale a set of nonnegative weights so they sum to exactly \(1\), turning "relative plausibility" numbers into genuine probabilities.
normalize_probs.formula: Divide each value by the sum of all values.
normalize_probs.example: `bayes_posterior`'s unnormalized weights \((0.0099,\,0.0495)\), summing to \(0.0594\) (matching `law_of_total_prob`'s overall positive-test probability exactly, as it must): normalized, \((0.0099/0.0594,\ 0.0495/0.0594) = (0.1667,\ 0.8333)\).
normalize_probs.why: This \(0.1667\) is the famous "base rate fallacy" result: even with a 99%-accurate test, a POSITIVE result only means about a 16.7% chance of actually having the (rare, 1%-prevalence) disease -- because the disease is so rare that the test's 5% false-positive rate, applied to the huge healthy majority, generates far more false alarms than true detections among the tiny sick minority. This is exactly why doctors don't diagnose from a single positive screening test alone.

bayes_log_posterior.intuition: The same prior-times-likelihood idea as `bayes_posterior`, but computed in LOG space (adding log-probabilities instead of multiplying raw probabilities) -- avoids numerical underflow when likelihoods are extremely small (multiplying many small probabilities together can underflow to exactly zero in floating point; adding their logarithms doesn't have this problem).
bayes_log_posterior.example: Same medical-test priors/likelihoods, in log space: \(\log(0.01)+\log(0.99)\approx-4.605+(-0.010)=-4.615\) for the disease hypothesis; \(\log(0.99)+\log(0.05)\approx-0.010+(-2.996)=-3.006\) for the no-disease hypothesis -- the SAME relative ordering as `bayes_posterior`'s raw computation (no-disease still more plausible), just expressed additively.
bayes_log_posterior.why: For a real classifier with many features and many hypotheses (`naive_bayes_classify`'s use case), multiplying dozens of small likelihood terms together in raw probability space would quickly underflow to exactly \(0.0\) in floating point -- working in log space (summing instead of multiplying) sidesteps that failure entirely.

naive_bayes_classify.intuition: Pick whichever class has the highest posterior probability, computed in log space (summing each feature's log-likelihood contribution independently -- the "naive" assumption is that features don't interact, so their log-likelihoods just add).
naive_bayes_classify.formula: Sum log-priors and per-feature log-likelihoods for each class; pick the class with the highest total.
naive_bayes_classify.example: Conceptually extends `bayes_log_posterior`'s single-feature example to MULTIPLE independent features -- each additional feature just contributes one more additive log-likelihood term to each class's running total, and whichever class's sum ends up largest is the predicted class.
naive_bayes_classify.why: The "naive" independence assumption is often technically wrong (real features usually DO interact somewhat) but works surprisingly well in practice -- it's a classic example of a deliberately simplified model that's cheap to compute and robust, rather than a theoretically perfect one.

markov_step.intuition: Given today's distribution of being in each state, apply the transition probabilities once to get tomorrow's distribution -- multiply the current state-distribution row-vector by the transition matrix.
markov_step.example: A simple weather model, states \(\{\text{Sunny},\text{Rainy}\}\), transition matrix \(T=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.1\\0.5&0.5\end{pmatrix}\) (90% sunny stays sunny; rainy is a 50/50 tossup). Starting certain it's sunny today, \(\pi=(1,0)\): tomorrow's distribution \(\pi'=(1\times0.9+0\times0.5,\ 1\times0.1+0\times0.5)=(0.9,\,0.1)\) -- a 90% chance of sun tomorrow, matching the transition matrix's own "sunny stays sunny" row directly (since today was certainly sunny).
markov_step.why: This \((0.9,0.1)\) becomes the STARTING point for `markov_run`'s example, which applies this same step again to see where the weather trends after two days instead of one.

markov_run.intuition: Apply `markov_step` repeatedly -- the distribution several days out, not just tomorrow.
markov_run.example: Continuing the weather example from \(\pi=(1,0)\): after 1 day, \((0.9,0.1)\) (from `markov_step`'s example). Apply the step again for day 2: \(\pi''_0=0.9\times0.9+0.1\times0.5=0.81+0.05=0.86\). \(\pi''_1=0.9\times0.1+0.1\times0.5=0.09+0.05=0.14\). So after 2 days: \((0.86,\,0.14)\).
markov_run.why: Notice the sunny-probability dropped from \(0.9\) (day 1) to \(0.86\) (day 2) -- trending DOWN toward `markov_stationary`'s long-run equilibrium value (\(5/6\approx0.833\), see its own example), since starting from "certainly sunny" is more extreme than the long-run typical weather pattern.

markov_stationary.intuition: No matter where you start, does the distribution eventually settle into a fixed, unchanging pattern? Find the distribution \(\pi^*\) that's already a FIXED POINT of the transition step -- applying `markov_step` to it gives back the exact same distribution.
markov_stationary.example: Same weather chain: solve \(\pi_0=0.9\pi_0+0.5\pi_1\) with \(\pi_0+\pi_1=1\). Substituting \(\pi_1=1-\pi_0\): \(\pi_0=0.9\pi_0+0.5(1-\pi_0)=0.4\pi_0+0.5\), so \(0.6\pi_0=0.5\), \(\pi_0=5/6\approx0.833\), \(\pi_1=1/6\approx0.167\) -- in the long run, this weather pattern is sunny about \(83.3\%\) of the time.
markov_stationary.why: Compare this stationary value (\(0.833\)) against `markov_run`'s trajectory starting from \((1,0)\): \(1\to0.9\to0.86\to\cdots\) -- steadily decreasing toward \(0.833\), confirming the iterative `markov_step` process really is converging toward this same fixed point, found here directly by solving an equation instead of iterating.

markov_is_absorbing_state.intuition: An absorbing state is one you can never LEAVE once you enter it -- its self-transition probability is exactly \(1\).
markov_is_absorbing_state.formula: Checks whether \(T_{ii}=1\) for the given state \(i\).
markov_is_absorbing_state.example: In the weather chain, is "Sunny" absorbing? \(T_{00}=0.9\), not \(1\) -- so no, there's always a chance of transitioning away to rainy. Neither state in this particular chain is absorbing.
markov_is_absorbing_state.why: An absorbing state would make `markov_stationary`'s long-run analysis trivial in a specific way -- if ANY state is absorbing, the chain eventually gets stuck there permanently (assuming it's reachable), and the "stationary distribution" degenerates to certainty on that one state, very different from this weather chain's genuine long-run MIX of sun and rain.

markov_tv_distance.intuition: How different are two probability distributions over the same states? Add up half the absolute difference at every state -- a common way to measure "distance" between two distributions.
markov_tv_distance.example: Compare `markov_step`'s day-1 distribution \(\pi=(0.9,0.1)\) against the stationary distribution \(q\approx(0.833,0.167)\): \(\delta = \tfrac12(|0.9-0.833|+|0.1-0.167|) = \tfrac12(0.067+0.067)=0.067\) -- a modest remaining gap after just one day.
markov_tv_distance.why: This \(0.067\) gap is exactly the kind of number `markov_mixing_steps` tracks over successive iterations, watching it shrink toward zero, to determine how many steps are needed before the chain is "close enough" to its long-run equilibrium to stop distinguishing it from the true stationary distribution.

markov_mixing_steps.intuition: How many steps does it take for a Markov chain, started from an arbitrary distribution, to get acceptably close to its stationary distribution? Repeatedly apply `markov_step`, checking `markov_tv_distance` against the stationary distribution after each one, until it drops below a given tolerance.
markov_mixing_steps.formula: Iterate `markov_step`, checking `markov_tv_distance` to the stationary distribution each time, until it's below `eps`.
markov_mixing_steps.example: For the weather chain starting at \((1,0)\): the TV distance to stationary was already down to \(0.067\) after just 1 step (from `markov_tv_distance`'s example) -- for a loose tolerance like \(\text{eps}=0.1\), this chain would already be considered "mixed" after just 1 step; a tighter tolerance would need a few more iterations to confirm.
markov_mixing_steps.why: This weather chain mixes FAST (within a handful of steps) because its transition probabilities are far from degenerate (no state is "sticky" in the extreme) -- a chain with probabilities very close to 0 or 1 (strong inertia to stay put) would take dramatically longer to forget its starting point and reach equilibrium.

markov_entropy_rate.intuition: How unpredictable is the CHAIN's long-run behavior, combining both how often each state is visited (the stationary distribution) and how uncertain the NEXT transition is from each state?
markov_entropy_rate.example: Weather chain, stationary \(\pi\approx(0.833,0.167)\): the Sunny row's own entropy is \(-(0.9\ln0.9+0.1\ln0.1)\approx-(-0.0948-0.2303)=0.3251\); the Rainy row's entropy is \(-(0.5\ln0.5+0.5\ln0.5)=\ln2\approx0.6931\) (a fair coin flip, maximum uncertainty). Weighted by how often each state occurs: \(h\approx0.833\times0.3251+0.167\times0.6931\approx0.2709+0.1157=0.3866\).
markov_entropy_rate.why: Notice the Rainy state's own transition entropy (\(0.693\), a coin flip) is much HIGHER than Sunny's (\(0.325\), fairly predictable) -- but because Sunny is visited far more often in the long run (\(83\%\) of the time), it dominates the overall weighted entropy rate more than its own individual unpredictability alone would suggest.

moving_average.intuition: Smooth out short-term noise by replacing each point with the average of it and its nearby neighbors -- a wider window smooths more aggressively but also lags further behind sudden real changes.
moving_average.formula: Each output point is the mean of the `window` most recent input points.
moving_average.example: Series \((1,3,2,4,3)\), window \(3\): first output \(=\text{mean}(1,3,2)=2\); second \(=\text{mean}(3,2,4)=3\); third \(=\text{mean}(2,4,3)=3\). Result: \((2,3,3)\) -- notice the output is SHORTER than the input (only 3 values from 5), since a full window of 3 doesn't fit until the 3rd position.
moving_average.why: The output being shorter than the input (by `window - 1` points) is a real, easy-to-forget detail -- code assuming the output is the same length as the input would misalign every subsequent calculation.

ema.intuition: Instead of a hard cutoff window (`moving_average`'s approach, where old points suddenly stop mattering at all once they fall outside the window), let every past point's influence decay smoothly and geometrically -- recent points matter more, but nothing is ever COMPLETELY forgotten.
ema.why: Unlike `moving_average`, this returns a value for EVERY input point (no shortened output) and reacts smoothly rather than having a value abruptly enter or leave a fixed window -- the tradeoff is that old data technically never fully disappears, just fades exponentially, which can be a feature or a subtle drawback depending on the application.

autocorrelation.intuition: Does this series correlate with a shifted (lagged) copy of itself? A strong positive autocorrelation at some lag means the series tends to repeat its own pattern that many steps later -- the signature of periodicity or persistence.
autocorrelation.example: Series \((1,3,2,4,3)\), mean \(2.6\), lag \(k=1\): deviations \((-1.6,\,0.4,\,-0.6,\,1.4,\,0.4)\). Numerator: \((-1.6)(0.4)+(0.4)(-0.6)+(-0.6)(1.4)+(1.4)(0.4) = -0.64-0.24-0.84+0.56=-1.16\). Denominator: \(1.6^2+0.4^2+0.6^2+1.4^2+0.4^2=2.56+0.16+0.36+1.96+0.16=5.2\). \(r_1=-1.16/5.2\approx-0.223\) -- a mild NEGATIVE lag-1 autocorrelation, meaning a high value tends to be followed by a slightly lower one on average in this short series.
autocorrelation.why: This is exactly `pearson_r`'s formula applied to a series against ITSELF, shifted -- autocorrelation is just ordinary correlation with a specific, structured pairing (each point against its own \(k\)-steps-later value) instead of two independent variables.

acf_vec.intuition: Compute `autocorrelation` at every lag from \(0\) up to some maximum, all at once -- the full "autocorrelation function", typically plotted to visually spot periodicity in a series.
acf_vec.formula: `autocorrelation` evaluated at every lag from \(0\) to `max_lag`.
acf_vec.example: For the same series, the lag-0 entry is always exactly \(1\) (any series is perfectly correlated with an UN-shifted copy of itself); the lag-1 entry is \(\approx-0.223\) (from `autocorrelation`'s own example); further lags would continue the pattern for as many steps as `max_lag` requests.
acf_vec.why: Plotting this whole vector (not just one lag) is the standard way to spot a series' periodicity -- a strong peak at some specific lag \(k>0\) suggests the series repeats a pattern roughly every \(k\) steps, information a single lag's value alone wouldn't reveal.

diff_series.intuition: How much did the series change from one step to the next? Subtracting consecutive values strips out a steady trend, leaving just the step-to-step fluctuations.
diff_series.why: This is the standard first step in time-series preprocessing to make a trending series more STATIONARY (statistically stable over time) before further analysis -- a series with a steady upward trend, once differenced, often looks like it's just fluctuating around a constant level instead.

cumsum.intuition: The running total as you walk through the series -- the exact operation that UNDOES differencing.
cumsum.why: `cumsum` and `diff_series` are exact inverses of each other (up to knowing the very first value) -- differencing a series and then cumulative-summing the result recovers the original series (offset by its starting value), a useful round-trip sanity check.

welford_mean_update.intuition: The same incremental-averaging idea [vani-calculus](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-calculus)'s `running_mean_update` uses -- nudge the running mean toward each new sample by a shrinking amount as more samples accumulate.
welford_mean_update.example: Streaming in \(D_1\)'s first two values, \(2\) then \(4\): after seeing \(2\) (\(n=1\)), mean is \(2\). Seeing \(4\) (\(n=2\)): \(\bar x_2 = 2+\dfrac{4-2}2=2+1=3\) -- matching the plain average \((2+4)/2=3\).
welford_mean_update.why: This update, together with `welford_m2_update`'s companion update, is the first half of Welford's numerically-stable ONE-PASS algorithm for computing both mean and variance together as data streams in, without ever storing the whole dataset.

welford_m2_update.intuition: Tracks a running sum-of-squared-deviations quantity (\(M_2\)) needed for variance, updated using BOTH the old and new mean together -- this specific two-mean formula is the key trick that keeps the computation numerically stable, avoiding the catastrophic cancellation a naive "sum of squares minus n times mean squared" formula risks.
welford_m2_update.example: Continuing from `welford_mean_update`'s example: seeing the second value \(x=4\), with old mean \(\bar x_{n-1}=2\), new mean \(\bar x_n=3\), old \(M_2=0\) (only one point seen so far, no spread yet): \(M_{2,2} = 0+(4-2)(4-3)=0+2\times1=2\).
welford_m2_update.why: This \(M_2=2\) is exactly what `welford_variance`'s example divides by \(n-1\) next to recover the actual sample variance -- notice the formula uses the OLD mean for one factor and the NEW mean for the other, not the same mean twice, which is precisely the detail that gives this algorithm its numerical stability advantage.

welford_variance.intuition: Once the running \(M_2\) accumulator is built up via `welford_m2_update`, recovering the actual sample variance is just one division -- the same Bessel-corrected \(n-1\) denominator ordinary `variance` uses.
welford_variance.example: \(M_2=2\), \(n=2\) (from `welford_m2_update`'s example): \(s^2=2/(2-1)=2\). Direct check: the two streamed values were \((2,4)\), mean \(3\); ordinary sample variance \(=\dfrac{(2-3)^2+(4-3)^2}{2-1}=\dfrac{1+1}1=2\) -- matches exactly.
welford_variance.why: This confirms Welford's streaming approach and the ordinary batch `variance` formula agree exactly -- the whole point of the streaming algorithm is getting the SAME correct answer while only ever looking at one data point at a time, never needing the full dataset in memory at once.

f_stat.intuition: Are two samples' spreads (variances) genuinely different, or close enough to be explained by chance? Take the RATIO of the two sample variances -- close to \(1\) suggests similar spread, far from \(1\) (in either direction) suggests a real difference.
f_stat.example: Two samples, \(x=(1,2,3)\) (variance \(1\)) and \(y=(4,5,6)\) (variance \(1\)): \(F=1/1=1\) -- the two samples have identical spread, even though their MEANS differ substantially (\(2\) vs \(5\), see `t_stat_two_sample`'s example on this same data).
f_stat.why: This is a genuinely different question from `t_stat_two_sample`'s: \(F\) asks "do these samples have the same SPREAD", while \(t\) asks "do these samples have the same CENTER" -- this example's two samples happen to agree on spread (\(F=1\), no evidence of different variance) while disagreeing substantially on center (a large \(|t|\)).

pooled_variance.intuition: When two samples are ASSUMED to share the same true underlying variance, combine their two separate variance estimates into one better, shared estimate -- weighted by each sample's own degrees of freedom.
pooled_variance.example: \(x=(1,2,3)\) (\(n_x=3\), \(s_x^2=1\)), \(y=(4,5,6)\) (\(n_y=3\), \(s_y^2=1\)): \(s_p^2 = \dfrac{2\times1+2\times1}{3+3-2}=\dfrac44=1\) -- unsurprising here since both individual variances were already equal to \(1\).
pooled_variance.why: This pooled value (\(1\)) is exactly what `t_stat_two_sample`'s example uses in its own denominator -- pooling only makes sense when you're willing to ASSUME equal population variances; when that assumption is shaky, `welch_df`'s adjustment is the safer alternative.

welch_df.intuition: When the two samples' variances DON'T look equal, pooling them (as `pooled_variance` does) is not appropriate -- Welch's formula instead computes an adjusted "effective" degrees of freedom that accounts for the mismatch, without assuming equal variances.
welch_df.example: Same \(x,y\) (equal variances \(1\), equal sizes \(3\)): \(\dfrac{(1/3+1/3)^2}{(1/3)^2/2+(1/3)^2/2} = \dfrac{(0.667)^2}{0.0556+0.0556}=\dfrac{0.444}{0.111}=4.0\) -- exactly matching the SIMPLE pooled degrees of freedom (\(n_x+n_y-2=4\)) that `pooled_variance`'s approach would use, because the variances here genuinely ARE equal.
welch_df.why: This match is expected: when the two samples' variances truly are equal, Welch's more cautious formula and the simpler pooled-variance approach agree -- Welch's adjustment only pulls the effective degrees of freedom LOWER (more conservative) when the variances genuinely differ, which isn't the case in this particular equal-variance example.

standardize.intuition: The single-vector version of z-score standardization -- shift to zero mean, rescale to unit spread.
standardize.example: Applied to \(D_1\) (mean \(5\), \(s\approx2.138\)): the value \(9\) standardizes to \((9-5)/2.138\approx1.871\) -- about 1.87 standard deviations above the mean.
standardize.why: This is the same core idea as [vani-ml](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-ml)'s `standardize_apply`, just operating directly on one plain `Vec<f64>` rather than fitting/applying a reusable `StandardScaler` across a whole feature matrix -- reach for THIS function for a quick one-off standardization, the ML package's scaler for a proper fit-once-apply-many-times pipeline.

mutual_information_discrete.intuition: How much does knowing one discrete variable's value reduce your uncertainty about another? Exactly zero when the two variables are genuinely INDEPENDENT (knowing one tells you nothing about the other); positive whenever there's some real association.
mutual_information_discrete.example: A joint distribution over two binary variables where every combination is equally likely, \(p(x,y)=0.25\) for all four combinations (so \(X\) and \(Y\) are genuinely independent, each marginal being \(0.5/0.5\)): \(I(X;Y) = 4\times0.25\times\ln\!\left(\dfrac{0.25}{0.5\times0.5}\right) = 4\times0.25\times\ln(1) = 0\) -- exactly zero, correctly detecting the independence.
mutual_information_discrete.why: This exact-zero result for a genuinely independent joint distribution is a useful sanity check on the formula itself -- mutual information is ALWAYS \(\ge0\), hitting exactly \(0\) if and only if the two variables are truly independent, never negative.

chi_squared_cdf.intuition: The cumulative probability version of `chi_squared_pdf` -- computed via the regularized incomplete gamma function in general, but with a clean closed form in the special \(k=2\) case.
chi_squared_cdf.formula: The chi-squared CDF, via the regularized incomplete gamma function.
chi_squared_cdf.example: At \(k=2\) (special case, identical to an exponential distribution): \(F(x)=1-e^{-x/2}\). At \(x=2\): \(1-e^{-1}\approx0.6321\) -- exactly matching `exponential_cdf`'s example value for \(\lambda=0.5\) at the same point.
chi_squared_cdf.why: This is `chi_squared_stat`'s test statistic's natural home -- once you have a chi-squared statistic, this CDF (via `chi_squared_pvalue`) is what converts it into an actual p-value for a goodness-of-fit or independence test.

gamma_cdf.intuition: The cumulative version of `gamma_pdf`, again via the regularized incomplete gamma function.
gamma_cdf.example: At `shape=1` (the exponential special case again): \(F(x)=1-e^{-\text{rate}\times x}\). With `rate=0.5`, \(x=2\): \(1-e^{-1}\approx0.6321\) -- matching `exponential_cdf`'s and `chi_squared_cdf`'s example values yet again, the same three-way identity chain from the PDF side carrying over to the CDF side.
gamma_cdf.why: This exact CDF machinery, generalized beyond `shape=1`, is what lets the Gamma distribution model "time until the \(k\)-th event" (not just the first) with a proper cumulative probability, unlike the exponential distribution's more limited single-event scope.

exponential_cdf_exact.intuition: The same formula as `exponential_cdf` -- this function exists as a separate, `_exact`-suffixed twin from an earlier phase of this package's development, before the systematic PDF/CDF naming pass paired every distribution consistently.
exponential_cdf_exact.example: Same \(\lambda=0.5\), \(x=2\): \(1-e^{-1}\approx0.6321\) -- identical to `exponential_cdf`'s answer, since it's the identical formula.
exponential_cdf_exact.why: Both functions exist and both are correct -- if you're not sure which to reach for, either works identically for the exponential distribution specifically; the `_exact` suffix here is a naming-history artifact, not a hint that one is more precise than the other.

t_cdf.intuition: The cumulative version of `t_pdf` -- what `t_stat_one_sample`/`t_stat_two_sample`'s test statistics get looked up against to determine statistical significance.
t_cdf.example: For a large number of degrees of freedom, `t_cdf` behaves almost identically to the standard normal CDF (\(\Phi\)) -- e.g. at \(t=1.96\) with many degrees of freedom, \(F(t)\) comes out very close to \(0.975\), the same landmark value the normal distribution gives at that point.
t_cdf.why: This convergence toward the normal distribution as degrees of freedom grows is exactly `t_pdf`'s own "why" note in action -- with enough data, the extra uncertainty from an ESTIMATED standard deviation becomes negligible, and the t-distribution's heavier tails shrink back down to match the normal's.

beta_cdf.intuition: The cumulative version of `beta_pdf`, via the regularized incomplete beta function.
beta_cdf.example: For the SYMMETRIC case \(\alpha=\beta=2\) (from `beta_pdf`'s example), evaluated at the exact midpoint \(x=0.5\): by symmetry alone (the density is a mirror image of itself around \(0.5\)), exactly half the total probability must lie below \(0.5\): \(F(0.5)=0.5\) exactly.
beta_cdf.why: This symmetry-implies-median-at-0.5 shortcut only holds because \(\alpha=\beta\) makes the distribution genuinely symmetric -- for ANY \(\alpha\ne\beta\), the distribution skews toward one end, and \(F(0.5)\) would no longer equal exactly \(0.5\).

f_cdf.intuition: The cumulative version of the F-distribution, which is what `f_stat`'s variance-ratio statistic gets compared against.
f_cdf.example: Using `f_stat`'s example (\(F=1\), from two samples with genuinely equal variances): a value of EXACTLY \(1\) sits right at the F-distribution's own median region for equal-sized samples -- neither variance estimate is dramatically bigger than the other, consistent with `f_stat`'s underlying samples truly having equal variance.
f_cdf.why: This CDF (via `f_pvalue`) is what turns `f_stat`'s raw ratio into an actual significance test for whether two samples' variances genuinely differ -- an \(F\) very close to \(1\), as in this example, would correspond to a large (non-significant) p-value, correctly failing to detect a variance difference that isn't really there.

t_pvalue_two_tailed.intuition: Converts a t-statistic into an actual probability: how likely would you be to see a t-statistic at least this EXTREME (in either direction), purely by chance, if there were really no difference at all?
t_pvalue_two_tailed.example: Using `t_stat_two_sample`'s \(t\approx-3.67\) (magnitude \(3.67\), with pooled degrees of freedom \(4\)): a t-statistic this large in magnitude, with so few degrees of freedom, corresponds to a fairly SMALL p-value -- comfortably below the common \(0.05\) significance threshold, suggesting these two samples' means really do differ meaningfully, not just by chance.
t_pvalue_two_tailed.why: The "two-tailed" in the name means this counts BOTH a t-statistic as extreme as \(+3.67\) AND as extreme as \(-3.67\) as equally surprising -- appropriate when you didn't have a specific DIRECTION of difference predicted in advance, just "are these different at all".

chi_squared_pvalue.intuition: Converts a chi-squared statistic into a p-value -- unlike the two-tailed t/z tests, chi-squared statistics are always non-negative, and "more extreme" only ever means "larger", so this is naturally one-tailed.
chi_squared_pvalue.example: Using `chi_squared_stat`'s example (\(\chi^2\approx3.33\) with \(2\) degrees of freedom, from 3 categories): this is a fairly modest chi-squared value for 2 degrees of freedom, corresponding to a p-value comfortably above the common \(0.05\) threshold -- not enough evidence here to conclude the observed counts genuinely differ from what was expected.
chi_squared_pvalue.why: Degrees of freedom for a goodness-of-fit test like `chi_squared_stat`'s example is (number of categories \(-1\)) -- here, 3 categories give 2 degrees of freedom, which is what this p-value lookup needs to know to correctly calibrate "how extreme is this statistic, for this many categories."

z_pvalue_two_tailed.intuition: Same two-tailed idea as `t_pvalue_two_tailed`, but looking up against the (simpler, single) standard normal distribution instead of the t-distribution family.
z_pvalue_two_tailed.example: Using `z_stat`'s example (\(z\approx1.414\)): \(\Phi(1.414)\approx0.9214\) (the standard normal CDF at this point). \(p=2\times(1-0.9214)=2\times0.0786\approx0.157\) -- well above the common \(0.05\) threshold, so this particular \(z\) wouldn't be considered statistically significant.
z_pvalue_two_tailed.why: Compare against `t_pvalue_two_tailed`'s much smaller p-value on a DIFFERENT example -- p-values depend heavily on both the statistic's magnitude AND the sample size/degrees of freedom behind it; a modest \(z\approx1.41\) here simply isn't extreme enough to rule out chance as the explanation.

f_pvalue.intuition: Converts an F-statistic into a p-value for testing whether two variances genuinely differ.
f_pvalue.example: Using `f_stat`'s example (\(F=1\), from two equal-variance samples): an \(F\) of exactly \(1\) is about as UNREMARKABLE as this statistic can be -- corresponding to a large p-value, correctly failing to find evidence of any real variance difference, consistent with the two samples' variances genuinely being equal in this example.
f_pvalue.why: This directly answers the "do these samples have different SPREAD" question `f_stat`'s own note poses -- a large p-value here (as expected for this example) means "no evidence of different spread", a separate conclusion from whatever `t_pvalue_two_tailed` might say about the samples' CENTERS.

mlr_fit.intuition: The multi-predictor generalization of `ols_slope`/`ols_intercept` -- rather than one simple formula, this solves the "normal equations" (a linear system derived from calculus, setting the gradient of the squared-error loss to zero) to find every coefficient at once.
mlr_fit.example: With a single predictor (the \(x,y\) data from `covariance`'s example, formatted as a one-column design matrix), `mlr_fit` should recover the SAME slope and intercept `ols_slope`/`ols_intercept` found directly (\(0.6\) and \(2.2\)) -- the general multi-predictor machinery reducing correctly to the simple-regression special case.
mlr_fit.why: Computed via [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s `mat_inv_n` rather than a specialized formula -- this is what lets `mlr_fit` scale to ANY number of predictors, unlike `ols_slope`/`ols_intercept`'s formulas, which are only valid for exactly one.

mlr_predict.intuition: Same idea as [vani-ml](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-ml)'s `linreg_predict` -- plug fitted coefficients back into the linear formula.
mlr_predict.example: Using `mlr_fit`'s recovered single-predictor coefficients (\(\hat\beta_0=2.2,\hat\beta_1=0.6\)) at \(x=3\): \(\hat y=2.2+0.6\times3=2.2+1.8=4.0\) -- matching the actual observed \(y=5\) reasonably closely but not exactly (since the fit isn't perfect for this noisy data), the expected behavior of a regression line through scattered points.
mlr_predict.why: The gap between this prediction (\(4.0\)) and the true observed value (\(5\)) at \(x=3\) is exactly the kind of residual `mlr_residuals` collects for every data point, which `mlr_r_squared` then summarizes into one overall fit-quality number.

mlr_residuals.intuition: How far off was each individual prediction from what actually happened? The raw leftover error at every data point.
mlr_residuals.example: Using the running \(x,y\) data and `mlr_fit`'s coefficients: at \(x=3\), actual \(y=5\), predicted \(\hat y=4.0\) (from `mlr_predict`'s example) -- residual \(=5-4.0=1.0\), a positive residual meaning the model UNDER-predicted at this specific point.
mlr_residuals.why: The sum of SQUARED residuals across every point is exactly \(SS_{\text{res}}\), the numerator `mlr_r_squared`'s formula needs -- residuals are the raw material every downstream fit-quality metric is built from.

mlr_r_squared.intuition: The general-case version of `ols_r_squared` -- computed directly from actual residuals rather than via the simple-regression \(r^2\) shortcut, since with multiple predictors there's no single correlation coefficient to square.
mlr_r_squared.example: For the single-predictor case (matching `ols_r_squared`'s setup exactly), `mlr_r_squared` computed the general way should recover the SAME answer, \(\approx0.6\), that `ols_r_squared`'s shortcut (\(r^2\)) found directly -- confirming the two routes agree when there's only one predictor to compare them on.
mlr_r_squared.why: Once there are MULTIPLE predictors, only this general residuals-based approach works at all -- `ols_r_squared`'s \(r^2\) shortcut has no multi-predictor equivalent, since Pearson correlation is inherently a two-variable-at-a-time concept.

mlr_adj_r_squared.intuition: Plain \(R^2\) can never DECREASE from adding another predictor, even a completely useless, random one -- which makes it a poor tool for deciding whether a new predictor is actually worth including. Adjusted \(R^2\) applies a penalty for each added predictor, so a genuinely useless one can make the adjusted score go DOWN even while plain \(R^2\) ticks up.
mlr_adj_r_squared.example: With \(R^2\approx0.6\), \(n=5\) observations, \(p=1\) predictor: \(R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1-(1-0.6)\times\dfrac{5-1}{5-1-1}=1-0.4\times\dfrac43=1-0.533\approx0.467\) -- noticeably LOWER than the unadjusted \(0.6\), reflecting the penalty for model complexity relative to this small sample size.
mlr_adj_r_squared.why: With only \(n=5\) data points and \(p=1\) predictor, the penalty is already substantial -- this gap between plain \(R^2\) (\(0.6\)) and adjusted \(R^2\) (\(0.467\)) would grow even larger if more predictors were added without a genuine improvement in fit, exactly the signal adjusted \(R^2\) is designed to surface.

cov_matrix.intuition: The multivariate generalization of `covariance` -- instead of one number for one pair of variables, compute EVERY pairwise covariance at once, including each variable's covariance with itself (which is just its own variance).
cov_matrix.example: For the running \(x,y\) data (var\(_x=2.5\), var\(_y=1.5\), cov\(=1.5\), all from earlier examples): \(\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2.5&1.5\\1.5&1.5\end{pmatrix}\) -- the diagonal holds each variable's own variance, the off-diagonal holds their shared covariance (appearing symmetrically on both sides).
cov_matrix.why: This matrix is exactly what `pca_power_iter` needs as its input -- PCA finds the DIRECTIONS (eigenvectors) in which this covariance structure spreads out the most, which is a matrix eigenvalue problem once you have this covariance matrix in hand.

correlation_matrix.intuition: The same idea as `cov_matrix`, but with every entry normalized by the relevant standard deviations -- the multivariate generalization of `pearson_r`, always \(1\) on the diagonal (a variable is always perfectly correlated with itself).
correlation_matrix.example: Using `cov_matrix`'s \(\Sigma\) and the same standard deviations (\(s_x\approx1.581,s_y\approx1.225\)): the off-diagonal entry becomes \(1.5/(1.581\times1.225)\approx0.775\) -- matching `pearson_r`'s own answer for this data exactly. The matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0.775\\0.775&1\end{pmatrix}\).
correlation_matrix.why: Unlike the raw covariance matrix (whose entries depend on each variable's own arbitrary scale/units), the correlation matrix's entries are always comparable and bounded in \([-1,1]\) -- useful for comparing the STRENGTH of association across pairs of variables that are measured in completely different units.

pca_power_iter.intuition: Finds the single DIRECTION in the data along which points are most spread out -- the first principal component -- using the exact same power-iteration idea [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s `mat_eig_power` uses for finding a dominant eigenvalue in general, just specifically applied to a covariance matrix.
pca_power_iter.formula: Power iteration on the covariance matrix, converging to its dominant eigenvector/eigenvalue.
pca_power_iter.example: For a covariance matrix like [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s own \(M_2=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) example (eigenvalues exactly \(1\) and \(3\), eigenvector \((1,1)/\sqrt2\) for the dominant \(\lambda=3\)): treating this AS a covariance matrix, PCA would find the first principal component pointing along \((1,1)\) -- meaning the two underlying variables tend to vary TOGETHER (both up or both down at once), the direction of maximum spread in the data.
pca_power_iter.why: This is LITERALLY `mat_eig_power` under a different name and a specific interpretation -- PCA's "find the direction of maximum variance" and eigenvalue decomposition's "find the dominant eigenvector" are the exact same mathematical operation, applied specifically to a covariance matrix.

pca_deflate.intuition: Same idea as [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s `mat_eig_deflate` -- remove the first principal component's contribution so a second round of `pca_power_iter` finds the SECOND principal component (the direction of maximum REMAINING spread, after accounting for the first) instead of re-finding the same one.
pca_deflate.formula: Subtract the found component's contribution (rank-1 update) from the covariance matrix.
pca_deflate.example: Continuing the \(M_2\) example: after deflating out the \((1,1)\)-direction (\(\lambda=3\)) component, a second `pca_power_iter` call on the deflated matrix would find the SECOND (and here, only remaining) principal component along \((1,-1)\), with eigenvalue \(1\) -- exactly [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s `mat_eig_deflate` example's own result.
pca_deflate.why: In a 2-variable problem like this, there are only 2 principal components total -- for higher-dimensional data, this deflate-and-repeat cycle continues, extracting one principal component at a time, each capturing the most remaining variance not already explained by the earlier ones.

random_walk_1d.intuition: Simulates a value that takes a small random step, up or down, at every tick -- like tracking a drunkard's position as they stumble randomly left or right with each step.
random_walk_1d.example: With \(\sigma=1\), starting at \(x_0=0\): each step adds a random draw from a standard normal distribution -- over many steps, the walk drifts further from \(0\) on average, but in an unpredictable (not steadily increasing or decreasing) direction, since each step's direction is independent of all previous ones.
random_walk_1d.why: A random walk's typical DISTANCE from the start grows proportionally to \(\sqrt{t}\) (not \(t\) itself) -- a well-known, slightly counterintuitive property: to expect to be twice as far from where you started, you need FOUR times as many steps, not just twice as many.

geometric_brownian.intuition: Models a quantity that can never go negative and whose PERCENTAGE changes (not absolute changes) are randomly distributed -- appropriate for prices, populations, or any quantity where a 1% move means the same relative thing whether the current value is small or large.
geometric_brownian.example: A starting value \(S_0=100\), drift \(\mu=0.05\) (5% average growth), volatility \(\sigma=0.2\): each simulated step multiplies the current value by a random factor centered slightly below \(e^{\mu \, dt}\) (the \(-\sigma^2/2\) correction accounts for the fact that multiplicative random fluctuations pull the AVERAGE of the exponentiated value down slightly relative to the plain drift rate) -- the value can wander up or down, but by construction can never cross zero.
geometric_brownian.why: This is the foundational model behind the Black-Scholes option-pricing formula -- "prices move by random PERCENTAGES, not random absolute amounts" is a much more realistic assumption for real financial markets than `random_walk_1d`'s plain additive randomness, which could (unrealistically) let a price wander below zero.

kalman_predict.intuition: Before you get a new measurement, what do you EXPECT the system's state to be, based purely on how it's known to evolve over time? Project the current best estimate forward using the system's dynamics, and grow the uncertainty a bit (since predictions always get less certain further into an unmeasured future).
kalman_predict.example: A simple static system (\(F=1\), the state doesn't change on its own), current estimate \(x=0\) with uncertainty \(P=1\), process noise \(Q=0.1\): predicted state \(x'=1\times0=0\) (unchanged, since \(F=1\)); predicted uncertainty \(P'=1\times1\times1+0.1=1.1\) -- slightly MORE uncertain than before, since some noise could have crept in even though the state itself isn't expected to move.
kalman_predict.why: This growing uncertainty (\(P=1\to P'=1.1\)) is exactly what `kalman_update`'s example reins back in once a new measurement arrives -- predict-then-update is the fundamental two-step cycle every Kalman filter runs, over and over, as new measurements arrive.

kalman_update.intuition: A new noisy measurement arrives -- blend it with the PREDICTED state from `kalman_predict`, weighted by how much you trust each source (a very confident prediction should barely move; a very noisy prediction should shift a lot toward what the measurement says).
kalman_update.formula: Kalman gain \(K=P'H^T(HP'H^T+R)^{-1}\); update \(\hat x\leftarrow\hat x+K(z-H\hat x)\), \(P\leftarrow(I-KH)P'\).
kalman_update.example: Continuing `kalman_predict`'s example (\(x'=0,P'=1.1\)), with a new measurement \(z=1\) (\(H=1\), measurement noise \(R=0.5\)): Kalman gain \(K=1.1/(1.1+0.5)=1.1/1.6\approx0.6875\). Updated state: \(x = 0+0.6875\times(1-0)=0.6875\) -- moved substantially toward the measurement (since the gain is fairly high, reflecting that the prediction's uncertainty \(1.1\) is larger than the measurement's uncertainty \(0.5\)). Updated uncertainty: \(P=(1-0.6875)\times1.1=0.3125\times1.1\approx0.344\) -- notably SMALLER than either the prediction's \(1.1\) or the measurement's \(0.5\) alone, since combining two independent, imperfect estimates always yields more confidence than either one by itself.
kalman_update.why: That final uncertainty (\(\approx0.344\)) being smaller than BOTH inputs is the whole point of the Kalman filter -- optimally combining a prediction and a measurement (both individually imperfect) yields a genuinely BETTER combined estimate than either source alone, not just an average of the two.

spearman_r.intuition: Instead of correlating the raw values (`pearson_r`'s approach, which only catches LINEAR relationships), correlate their RANKS -- this catches any consistently increasing or decreasing relationship, even a curved one, as long as it's monotonic.
spearman_r.formula: `pearson_r` computed on the ranks of the data instead of the raw values.
spearman_r.example: \(x=(1,2,3,4,5)\) (already in rank order) and \(y=(5,3,4,2,1)\) (ranks, since \(y\) is already a permutation of \(1\)-\(5\)): computing `pearson_r` on \(x\) against these ranks: covariance \(=-9/4=-2.25\), both variances \(=2.5\), giving \(r=-2.25/2.5=-0.9\) -- a strong negative rank correlation, correctly reflecting that \(y\) trends DOWN overall as \(x\) increases, even though it's not a perfectly straight-line relationship (there's a slight zigzag: \(5,3,4,2,1\) dips then rises then falls again).
spearman_r.why: A relationship that curves consistently upward or downward (but isn't a straight line) can score a WEAKER `pearson_r` than its true strength of association deserves, while `spearman_r` -- caring only about the consistent ranking, not the exact shape -- captures the full strength of any monotonic relationship, straight or curved.

mann_whitney_u_stat.intuition: A rank-based alternative to `t_stat_two_sample` that doesn't assume the data is normally distributed -- pool both samples together, rank everything, and compare how the ranks from each original sample are distributed.
mann_whitney_u_stat.formula: A rank-sum-based statistic testing whether two samples come from the same distribution.
mann_whitney_u_stat.example: For two samples that are clearly separated (e.g. one sample's values all rank lower than the other's, like \(x=(1,2,3)\) vs \(y=(4,5,6)\)), the Mann-Whitney statistic would take on an extreme value reflecting that separation -- similar in spirit to how `t_stat_two_sample`'s large \(|t|\approx3.67\) on this same data reflects a big difference, but without assuming either sample follows a normal distribution.
mann_whitney_u_stat.why: Reach for this instead of `t_stat_two_sample` when you're not confident the data is normally distributed, or when it contains outliers that would disproportionately affect a mean-based test -- ranks are inherently robust to exactly that kind of distortion.

kolmogorov_smirnov_stat.intuition: Compares two samples' entire empirical CUMULATIVE distributions, not just a single summary number like a mean or rank-sum -- the statistic is the single BIGGEST vertical gap between the two samples' empirical CDFs, anywhere along the number line.
kolmogorov_smirnov_stat.formula: The maximum absolute difference between two samples' empirical CDFs.
kolmogorov_smirnov_stat.example: Two small samples, \(x=(1,2,3)\) and \(y=(2,3,4)\): at the value \(1\), \(x\)'s empirical CDF has already reached \(1/3\) while \(y\)'s is still at \(0\) -- a gap of \(1/3\). At \(4\), \(x\)'s CDF is at \(1\) (fully accounted for) while \(y\)'s just reached \(1\) too -- no gap there. The overall KS statistic is the LARGEST such gap found across every point, capturing wherever the two samples' distributions differ most.
kolmogorov_smirnov_stat.why: Because it looks at the WHOLE distribution shape (not just means, medians, or ranks), the KS test can detect differences in SPREAD or SHAPE between two samples that a test only sensitive to central tendency (like `t_stat_two_sample` or `mann_whitney_u_stat`) might completely miss.
